query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In dilute Pt‐doped Cu catalysts, the extent of electronic modification (specifically, the shift in the d‐band center of surface Cu atoms) and the resultant catalytic hydrogenation activity are quantitatively dictated by the depth at which Pt dopant atoms reside. Subsurface Pt dopants located in the first or second atomic layers induce an optimal ligand effect that lowers the hydrogen dissociation barrier and enhances selectivity (favoring partial hydrogenation of unsaturated aldehydes), whereas Pt dopants on the extreme surface or deeper than two layers produce either excessive or insufficient electronic modulation.
generation.material_initial_state: Well‐defined Cu thin films synthesized with a very low (sub-1 at.%) concentration of Pt, where the Pt atoms are incorporated at controlled depths (surface layer, first subsurface layer, second subsurface layer, and deeper layers) on an inert support.
generation.intervention: Synthesize a series of model Cu catalysts with identical overall Pt loading but with Pt atoms selectively positioned at varying depths (using techniques such as atomic layer deposition followed by controlled overlayer growth or ion implantation with subsequent annealing) and then test their performance in a hydrogenation reaction.
generation.conditions: Conduct catalytic hydrogenation of an unsaturated aldehyde (e.g., cinnamaldehyde) under mild, controlled temperature and pressure conditions (e.g., ambient to moderate temperatures, 1–5 atm H2) while performing in situ electronic structure measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: The dopant depth modulates the surface electronic structure by shifting the d‐band center of Cu, which can be directly monitored via in situ ambient-pressure XPS or UPS.
generation.mechanism: Pt dopants located in the subsurface region induce a favorable ligand (electronic) effect that gradually decays with increased depth. When Pt is just below the surface (first to second atomic layers), the induced shift in the d‐band center of Cu optimally reduces the activation barrier for H2 dissociation and adjusts the adsorption energies of reaction intermediates. In contrast, Pt atoms at the outermost surface may over-modify the adsorption energies (potentially leading to undesired over-hydrogenation), while deeply buried dopants are too remote to effectively alter the surface electronic structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: A clear, monotonic trend will be observed: catalysts with Pt dopants in the first or second subsurface layer will show a pronounced negative shift in the d‐band center compared to pure Cu, correlate with lower hydrogen dissociation activation energies, and display enhanced selectivity toward partial hydrogenation products (e.g., unsaturated alcohols). Catalysts with Pt at the surface or in deeper layers will exhibit less optimal electronic modification and poorer catalytic performance.
generation.baseline: Pure Cu catalyst (no Pt dopant) and catalysts with identical overall Pt content but with uncontrolled dopant distribution.
generation.boundary: This quantitative dopant depth effect is expected to hold for dilute alloy systems of low-concentration Pt in coinage metals under mild hydrogenation conditions and may not extend to higher dopant concentrations, different metal combinations, or reaction environments with strong metal-support interactions.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the findings reported in the Pt-doped Cu study (e.g., PMC11075014) by explicitly quantifying the influence of dopant depth on d-band center shifts—a factor that the traditional isolated atom model has neglected. While the previous results indicate subsurface Pt can modulate surface Cu electronic structure, the precise depth‐dependent trend and its influence on activation barriers and selectivity remain unquantified. Uncertainties include potential influences from support interactions and dopant clustering, which need to be minimized. Additionally, combining insights from d-band theory studies in strain-modulated systems (e.g., PMC9419203) with recent subsurface dopant evidence provides the rationale for this hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of model Cu catalysts with a fixed, dilute Pt loading where the Pt dopant depth is systematically varied (confirmed by cross-sectional TEM and depth-profiling XPS). Measure the d‐band center position of surface Cu atoms using in situ UPS or ambient-pressure XPS under reaction conditions. Conduct catalytic hydrogenation of cinnamaldehyde and quantify reaction kinetics (turnover frequencies, activation energies) and selectivity to unsaturated alcohols.
measurements: Dopant depth confirmation via cross-sectional STEM and depth-profiling XPS
In situ determination of the d-band center shift of surface Cu atoms (UPS/XPS)
Kinetic parameters of H2 dissociation and overall hydrogenation rates
Product distribution and selectivity analysis (e.g., gas chromatography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant correlation between the controlled Pt dopant depth, the measured d-band center shift, and the catalytic performance (activation barrier and product selectivity) compared to the pure Cu baseline, then the hypothesis that dopant depth governs the electronic structure modification and thereby the catalytic mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWith heterogeneous catalysts, chemical promotion takes place at their surfaces. Even in the case of single-atom alloys, where small quantities of a reactive metal are dispersed within the main host, it is assumed that both elements are exposed and available to bond with the reactants. Here, we show, on the basis of in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy data, that in alloy catalysts made from Pt highly diluted in Cu the Pt atoms are located at the inner interface between the metal nanoparticles and the silica support instead. Kinetic experiments indicated that these catalysts still display better selectivity for the hydrogenation of unsaturated aldehydes to unsaturated alcohols than the pure metals. A couple of observations are worth highlighting from those results.
